cards.front: Living things need carbon because it is in their {{c1::sugar, fat and protein}}.
cards.quote: Living things need carbon: it is in their sugar, fat and protein.
cards.section: Explain: the flows in and out of the tub

cards.front: {{c1::Photosynthesis}} is the process in which plants, algae and some bacteria use light energy to make sugar from carbon dioxide and water.
cards.back: It takes carbon out of the air.
cards.quote: Photosynthesis is the process in which plants, algae and some bacteria use radiant energy (light energy, such as sunlight) to make sugar (glucose) from carbon dioxide and water.
cards.section: Explain: the flows in and out of the tub

cards.front: {{c1::Respiration}} is the process in which cells break down sugar and release carbon dioxide and water.
cards.back: Plants, animals and decomposers all do it.
cards.quote: Respiration is the process in which cells break down sugar and release carbon dioxide and water.
cards.section: Explain: the flows in and out of the tub

cards.front: {{c1::Decomposition}} is the breakdown of dead organisms and wastes by decomposers such as bacteria and fungi.
cards.back: It returns carbon to the air and the soil.
cards.quote: Decomposition is the breakdown of dead organisms and wastes by decomposers such as bacteria and fungi.
cards.section: Explain: the flows in and out of the tub

cards.front: {{c1::Transpiration}} is the release of water vapor from plant leaves, through tiny openings.
cards.back: The water comes up from the roots.
cards.quote: Transpiration is the release of water vapor from plant leaves, through tiny openings; the water comes up from the roots.
cards.section: Explain: water moves, and plants help move it

cards.front: Name the six water cycle processes in this unit.
cards.back: Evaporation, condensation, precipitation, infiltration, runoff and transpiration.
cards.quote: You learned the water cycle in grade 6. Here are six important processes in it.
cards.section: Explain: water moves, and plants help move it

cards.front: In the "tub of carbon" idea, when does the carbon dioxide in the air go up, and when does it go down?
cards.back: It goes up only when more flows in than flows out. It goes down only when more flows out than flows in.
cards.quote: The carbon dioxide in the air goes up only when more flows in than flows out, and down only when more flows out than flows in.

cards.front: Plants respire day and night. Why can the carbon dioxide in northern air still fall in summer?
cards.back: Photosynthesis takes carbon out of the air faster than respiration, decomposition and burning put it back, so more flows out than in.
cards.why: The tub rule: the level follows which flow is bigger.
cards.quote: Plants, animals and decomposers all do it, day and night.
cards.section: Explain: the flows in and out of the tub

cards.front: Why does burning coal, oil or natural gas add carbon to the air instead of just moving carbon already in the cycle?
cards.back: These fuels formed from living things that died long ago. Their carbon sat underground for millions of years, so burning adds carbon that was stored out of the cycle.
cards.quote: Coal, oil and natural gas formed from living things that died long ago, so burning them adds carbon that sat underground for millions of years.
cards.section: Explain: the flows in and out of the tub

cards.front: Where does most of the water vapor in the air come from, and what drives the change?
cards.back: Most evaporates from the ocean. Heat from the Sun turns liquid water into vapor.
cards.quote: Most of the water vapor in the air evaporates from the ocean.
cards.section: Explain: water moves, and plants help move it

cards.front: Rain falls on a hillside. What is the difference between infiltration and runoff?
cards.back: Infiltration is water soaking into the ground. Runoff is water flowing over the land into streams and rivers, pulled downhill by gravity.
cards.quote: Infiltration is water soaking into the ground. Runoff is water flowing over the land into streams and rivers.
cards.section: Explain: water moves, and plants help move it

cards.front: A student says energy cycles through an ecosystem like carbon and water. What is the best reply?
cards.back: Not quite. Matter such as carbon and water is reused, but energy comes in as sunlight and leaves as heat.
cards.quote: Energy is the one thing that does not cycle; you traced its flow in Food Webs and Energy.
cards.section: Explain: how the cycles connect

cards.front: In the carbon model, you cut down the trees. Predict what happens to the summer dip in the air's carbon dioxide.
cards.back: In the model, the dip should get smaller. With fewer plants, less carbon should flow out of the air by photosynthesis in summer.
cards.why: Rests on the tub rule: the dip comes from outflow beating inflow.
cards.quote: Predict whether the summer dip gets bigger or smaller and whether the lowest month for carbon dioxide moves.
cards.section: Explore: run the tub

cards.front: In the carbon model, burning is set to None and the model runs ten years. What happens to the yearly rise and fall, and to the long-term climb?
cards.back: The yearly rise and fall should mostly stay, since plants mostly cause it. The long climb should largely stop, since the extra carbon from burning is gone. Check by running it.
cards.why: Tub rule: the level climbs only when more flows in than out.
cards.quote: When people add carbon faster than plants and the ocean take it up, the amount in the air rises.
cards.section: Explain: why Hawaii’s air follows the northern seasons

cards.front: At Mauna Loa, carbon dioxide was 430.51 ppm in May 2025 and 424.37 ppm in September 2025. What was the change, and what does it say about the flows?
cards.back: 424.37 − 430.51 = −6.14 ppm, a fall of about 6 ppm. More carbon flowed out of the air (plant uptake) than flowed in.
cards.quote: The rise slows from April to May, then turns into a fall as northern leaves open.
cards.section: Explain: why Hawaii’s air follows the northern seasons

cards.front: Mauna Loa read 317.51 ppm in May 1958 and 430.51 ppm in May 2025. About how much did the record climb each year on average?
cards.back: 430.51 − 317.51 = 113 ppm over 67 years, about 1.7 ppm a year.
cards.why: Same month each year, so the yearly swing cancels.
cards.quote: But those months sit at different points of the yearly swing.
cards.section: Elaborate: a year of air at Mauna Loa

cards.front: A Virginia forest gets almost no rain for a whole summer. What most likely happens to its carbon cycle, and why?
cards.back: The trees take in less carbon dioxide. Photosynthesis uses water and carbon dioxide together, so less water means less photosynthesis.
cards.quote: Photosynthesis uses water and carbon dioxide together, so a change in one cycle can change the other.
cards.section: Explain: how the cycles connect

cards.front: A class wraps the soil of two potted plants in plastic. One plant has leaves, the other had its leaves removed. After two days the leafy pot lost 48 g and the leafless pot lost 6 g. What does this show?
cards.back: Most of the water left through the leaves, by transpiration. The plastic stops soil water escaping, so the extra 42 g lost by the leafy plant left through its leaves.
cards.quote: so water can leave only through the plant, wrap the soil surface in plastic
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: At Mauna Loa the level was 424.37 ppm in September 2025 and 427.49 ppm in December 2025. What happened, and what does it mean for the flows in and out?
cards.back: It rose about 3.1 ppm. More carbon flowed into the air than flowed out.
cards.why: Tub rule: a rise means inflow beat outflow.
cards.quote: Reminder: the level goes up only when more flows in than out.
cards.section: Explain: why Hawaii’s air follows the northern seasons

cards.front: Mauna Loa is in the middle of the Pacific Ocean. Why does its air follow the seasons of land plants far away?
cards.back: It is in the Northern Hemisphere, where most land and land plants are. Air mixes across the north, so northern plants set the yearly pattern.
cards.quote: Air moves and mixes across the north, so northern plants set the beat.
cards.section: Explain: why Hawaii’s air follows the northern seasons

cards.front: Plan a fair test: do plants in bright light lose more water through transpiration than plants in shade? Name the variables and a control.
cards.back: Change: light (lamp or shaded shelf). Measure: pot mass lost in grams after 48 hours. Keep the same: plant, pot, soil, watering, room temperature. Control: a pot of wet soil with no plant in each place. Wrap the soil in plastic so water leaves only through the plant.
cards.quote: Question: Do plants in bright light lose more water by transpiration than plants in shade?
cards.section: Design problem

cards.front: How does one leaf link the water cycle and the carbon cycle, and why can a change in one cycle change the other?
cards.back: The tiny openings that let carbon dioxide in also let water vapor out. Photosynthesis uses water and carbon dioxide together, so a change in one can change the other.
cards.quote: The water cycle runs alongside and meets the carbon cycle at the tiny openings in leaves.
